pillar: Gene Therapy for Inherited Blood Disorders: Beyond Thalassaemia

groups.title: Understanding Gene Therapy for Blood Disorders

items.q: What is gene therapy for inherited blood disorders like thalassaemia and sickle cell disease?
items.a: Gene therapy for inherited blood disorders is a one-time treatment that corrects or compensates for the faulty gene causing conditions such as beta-thalassaemia and sickle cell disease, aiming to remove the lifelong need for transfusions or medication rather than simply managing symptoms. Three main approaches are in use: lentiviral gene addition, which inserts a working gene copy into a patient's own stem cells (used in Zynteglo and Lyfgenia); CRISPR-Cas9 gene editing, which reactivates foetal haemoglobin production (used in Casgevy); and AAV-mediated gene transfer, which delivers a missing clotting factor gene directly to the liver in haemophilia. Whether gene therapy is the right option for a specific patient depends on genotype, disease severity, organ function, and review by a qualified haematology team.

items.q: Which inherited blood disorders can be treated with gene therapy or gene-edited stem cell therapy?
items.a: Gene therapy or gene-edited stem cell therapy is currently being used or trialled for seven inherited blood disorders: beta-thalassaemia major, sickle cell disease, haemophilia A, haemophilia B, Fanconi anaemia, Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome, and ADA-SCID. Each disorder is linked to a specific gene defect — for example, HBB mutations in thalassaemia and sickle cell disease, F8 or F9 mutations in haemophilia A and B, and ADA gene mutations in ADA-SCID — and treatment options range from approved products like Casgevy and Hemgenix to ongoing clinical trials. Suitability for any of these therapies depends on the genotype confirmed by DNA mutation analysis, disease severity, and assessment by a specialist team, and should not be assumed from the diagnosis name alone.

items.q: How does CRISPR gene editing work in a therapy like Casgevy?
items.a: CRISPR gene editing in Casgevy works by using a guide RNA to direct the Cas9 enzyme to a specific site in the patient's own stem cells, where it disrupts the BCL11A erythroid enhancer to switch foetal haemoglobin production back on and compensate for the missing or defective adult haemoglobin. This differs from lentiviral gene addition because it edits the patient's existing DNA rather than inserting a new gene copy, and no donor cells are required. In pivotal trials, 93% of transfusion-dependent thalassaemia patients and 97% of sickle cell disease patients treated with Casgevy achieved the trial's primary outcome at 12 months, though individual results vary and eligibility is confirmed only after specialist review.

items.q: What is the difference between gene therapy and an allogeneic bone marrow transplant?
items.a: The main difference is that gene therapy uses a patient's own modified stem cells and does not require a donor, while an allogeneic bone marrow transplant uses stem cells from a matched or half-matched donor and carries a risk of graft-versus-host disease (GvHD) that gene therapy avoids. Allogeneic transplant has a four-decade track record and is accessible today in India and China from an estimated USD 20,000–60,000 depending on donor match, while approved gene therapies such as Casgevy, Zynteglo, and Lyfgenia cost an estimated USD 2.1–3.1 million commercially, with lower-cost trial access developing in China. Both approaches may offer the possibility of cure, but the right choice depends on donor availability, patient age, organ function, and cost, and should be decided with a specialist haematology team.

items.q: Who is eligible for gene therapy for thalassaemia or sickle cell disease?
items.a: Eligibility for gene therapy generally requires a DNA mutation-confirmed diagnosis — such as a beta0/beta0 or severe beta0/beta+ genotype for transfusion-dependent thalassaemia, or a homozygous HbSS genotype for sickle cell disease — along with adequate organ function to tolerate the myeloablative conditioning used before the modified cells are reinfused. Age, transfusion history, iron overload, and prior treatment are also reviewed as part of eligibility screening, and criteria differ between approved products and clinical trials. Because eligibility is disorder-specific and depends on genetic profile, organ function, and specialist review, it should always be confirmed directly with the treating haematology team rather than assumed from a diagnosis alone.

items.q: What is the Pesaro classification and why does it matter for a bone marrow transplant?
items.a: The Pesaro classification is a three-tier risk system (Class I, II, or III) used to stratify thalassaemia patients before allogeneic transplant, based on the adequacy of prior iron chelation, presence of an enlarged liver, and presence of portal fibrosis on liver biopsy. Class I patients, with none of these adverse factors, achieve overall survival above 90% at expert centres, while Class III patients face significantly lower cure rates and higher transplant-related risk. Pesaro class helps guide the decision of whether and when to transplant, the intensity of the conditioning regimen, and the choice of treatment centre, and should be assessed and interpreted by the treating haematology and transplant team.

items.q: What medical tests are needed before applying for a gene therapy clinical trial?
items.a: Before applying for a gene therapy clinical trial, patients typically need DNA mutation confirmation of their genotype, a complete blood count with reticulocyte count, ferritin and MRI-based liver iron concentration, a cardiac T2* MRI for patients with a long transfusion history, a full organ function panel, foetal haemoglobin level, and a bone marrow biopsy to confirm cellularity. These tests establish disease severity and confirm that the patient meets the trial's genetic and organ-function eligibility criteria before a case is submitted to the trial's principal investigators. Because requirements vary by trial and centre, and final eligibility is determined only after investigator review, patients should confirm the exact test list with the specific trial centre rather than assuming it is identical everywhere.

items.q: What are the risks and possible side effects of gene therapy for blood disorders?
items.a: The main risks of gene therapy for inherited blood disorders come from the myeloablative conditioning chemotherapy (typically busulfan-based) used to prepare the bone marrow before treatment, which can cause organ toxicity, infertility, and a small increased risk of secondary blood cancers over time. Because gene therapy uses the patient's own modified cells, it avoids the graft-versus-host disease seen in donor transplants, but it is not risk-free and requires an extended hospital stay and monitoring period. Gene therapy is not guaranteed to work for every patient or genotype, and its risks and suitability should be discussed in detail with a qualified haematology team before proceeding.

items.q: What is the Beijing Protocol and how safe is a haploidentical transplant?
items.a: The Beijing Protocol is a haploidentical (half-matched) transplant technique developed at Peking University People's Hospital that combines a G-CSF-primed bone marrow and peripheral blood stem cell graft with intensified immunosuppression to achieve reliable engraftment without requiring a fully matched donor. It expands transplant access to virtually any parent or most siblings when no matched sibling donor is available, but chronic graft-versus-host disease still occurs in a meaningful proportion of allogeneic transplants generally, and close post-transplant monitoring is required. The safety and suitability of a haploidentical approach for a specific patient depends on donor characteristics, disease severity, and organ function, and should be evaluated by an experienced transplant team.

items.q: How much does gene therapy cost for thalassaemia and sickle cell disease?
items.a: Approved gene therapies for thalassaemia and sickle cell disease cost an estimated USD 2.1–3.1 million commercially in the United States — Zynteglo around USD 2.8 million, Lyfgenia around USD 3.1 million, and Casgevy around USD 2.2 million — while gene therapy clinical trials in China, where the investigational drug is typically trial-funded, involve estimated non-drug costs of roughly USD 15,000–40,000 for workup, conditioning, and monitoring. These figures are estimated ranges only, and actual costs depend on the specific product, trial, hospital, and length of stay. Final cost estimates and financing options should always be confirmed directly with the treating centre before a decision is made.

items.q: How much does a bone marrow transplant cost at CMC Vellore in India?
items.a: A matched sibling donor (MSD) allogeneic stem cell transplant for thalassaemia at CMC Vellore costs an estimated USD 20,000–30,000 for the full treatment package, including conditioning, the transplant itself, four to six weeks of inpatient care, and initial post-transplant follow-up, while a haploidentical transplant is estimated at USD 30,000–45,000. These figures compare with an estimated USD 300,000–700,000 for equivalent transplants in Western Europe or the United States. Costs are estimates only and can vary with a patient's specific protocol, complications, and length of stay, so exact pricing should be confirmed directly with the hospital's international patient team.

items.q: Which countries offer accessible treatment for inherited blood disorders?
items.a: India and China currently offer the most accessible treatment pathways for inherited blood disorders, with India's CMC Vellore, AIIMS Delhi, and Apollo Hospitals network providing allogeneic stem cell transplant at a fraction of Western costs, and China's Zhejiang University, Guangzhou Women and Children's Medical Centre, Peking University People's Hospital, and CAMS Institute of Hematology offering both transplant and gene therapy clinical trial access. Availability of a specific treatment depends on the disorder, the patient's genotype and organ function, and each centre's own eligibility criteria. Hospital acceptance, trial enrolment, and visa approval are never guaranteed and should be confirmed directly with the treating institution.

items.q: Is lifelong blood transfusion more or less expensive than a one-time curative treatment?
items.a: Over a 20-year period, lifelong transfusion and iron chelation for a thalassaemia major patient is estimated to cost roughly USD 40,000–80,000 in India or USD 400,000–800,000 in Western Europe, which can exceed the estimated cost of a one-time curative allogeneic transplant in India or China (roughly USD 20,000–60,000) even though transfusion alone never resolves the underlying condition. Commercial gene therapies remain far more expensive upfront at an estimated USD 2.1–3.1 million. These are estimated ranges only, and the most cost-effective path for a given patient depends on disease severity, donor availability, and treatment eligibility, and should be discussed with the treating haematology team.

items.q: Can international patients join gene therapy clinical trials in China?
items.a: Yes, international patients can be considered for gene therapy clinical trials in China, where NMPA-approved investigational trials typically permit international enrolment subject to eligibility criteria and principal investigator approval, and patients from South Asia, Southeast Asia, the Middle East, and Africa have previously enrolled at centres such as Zhejiang University and Guangzhou Women and Children's Medical Centre. Trial drug costs are usually covered, while patients bear an estimated USD 15,000–40,000 in workup, conditioning, and monitoring costs. Enrolment is never guaranteed and depends on genotype, disease severity, and investigator review, so cases should be submitted for formal eligibility assessment before travel is arranged.

items.q: Which hospitals in China are researching gene therapy for inherited blood disorders?
items.a: Four centres lead China's gene therapy and advanced transplant research for inherited blood disorders: Zhejiang University First Affiliated Hospital, which conducted the world's first human CRISPR trial for beta-thalassaemia in 2019 and now runs expanded Phase I/II gene editing trials; Guangzhou Women and Children's Medical Centre, China's leading paediatric haemoglobinopathy centre; Peking University People's Hospital, home of the haploidentical Beijing Protocol; and CAMS Institute of Hematology in Tianjin, which runs trials in sickle cell disease and rare blood disorders. Referral to any of these centres does not guarantee trial acceptance, which depends on genotype, disease severity, and investigator review.

items.q: What is base editing and how is it different from CRISPR gene editing?
items.a: Base editing is a next-generation gene editing technique that converts one DNA base directly into another without creating the double-strand breaks used in standard CRISPR-Cas9 editing, which may reduce the risk of unintended chromosomal changes, while a related technique called prime editing uses a guide RNA to write specific new DNA sequences directly. Groups such as China's CorrectSequence Therapeutics and academic teams at Peking University are advancing these approaches in thalassaemia research. Base and prime editing remain earlier-stage or trial technologies rather than approved treatments, and their availability and suitability for a specific patient depend on ongoing trial eligibility and specialist review.

items.q: What were the clinical trial results for Casgevy, Zynteglo, and Lyfgenia?
items.a: In pivotal trials, Casgevy achieved 93% transfusion independence at 12 months in transfusion-dependent thalassaemia (CLIMB-111) and 97% freedom from severe vaso-occlusive crises in sickle cell disease (CLIMB-121); Zynteglo's Northstar-3 trial reported transfusion independence in 89% of non-beta0/beta0 thalassaemia patients; and Lyfgenia's HGB-206 trial reported complete resolution of vaso-occlusive events in 88% of sickle cell disease patients. These results come from specific pivotal trial populations, and outcomes for an individual patient can differ based on genotype, disease severity, and prior treatment. Suitability for any of these approved therapies should be assessed by a qualified haematology specialist.

items.q: Should my child have a bone marrow transplant now or wait for a gene therapy trial?
items.a: For a child with an HLA-matched sibling donor and favourable Pesaro Class I or II status, allogeneic stem cell transplant at a centre such as CMC Vellore or Peking University may be considered today with survival rates above 90% in this group, while gene therapy trials in China are generally considered for patients without a matched sibling donor and involve a three-to-six month process to confirm enrolment. Neither path is automatically the better choice, and the decision depends on donor availability, organ function, Pesaro class, family preference, and current trial eligibility. This decision should be made jointly with the treating haematology and transplant team after reviewing all available options.

items.q: How long is the hospital stay and recovery after a stem cell transplant or gene therapy?
items.a: Allogeneic stem cell transplant typically involves four to six weeks of inpatient care at centres like CMC Vellore, followed by close monitoring for engraftment and graft-versus-host disease over six to twelve months, while autologous gene therapy also requires an extended admission for cell collection, conditioning, and reinfusion followed by a comparable recovery and monitoring period. Exact timelines vary with the specific protocol, conditioning regimen, and any complications that arise. Because recovery length affects travel planning, accommodation, and follow-up care, patients and families should confirm expected timelines directly with the treating centre before finalising travel arrangements.

items.q: How does CancerFax help families access gene therapy or transplant for inherited blood disorders?
items.a: CancerFax helps patients organize medical reports, identify relevant specialists or trials, estimate costs, and coordinate travel, visa, and follow-up support alongside the treating oncology team. For inherited blood disorders specifically, this includes verifying molecular diagnosis, reviewing Pesaro class and transplant eligibility, coordinating HLA typing and donor searches through Indian and Chinese registries, and submitting cases for gene therapy trial eligibility screening at centres such as Zhejiang University and Guangzhou Women and Children's Medical Centre. CancerFax does not replace the treating haematology team, and all final treatment decisions, trial enrolment, and hospital acceptance remain subject to the specialist medical team's review.
